5. Josh Dunkley, 8.5/10 -- Could not have played a more inspirational game if he tried. In and under throughout with 14 contested possessions and 12 tackles. Smothers. Spoils. Gut-busting runs. He did everything. Easily could have won the Norm Smith Medal.

6. Hugh McCluggage, 5/10 -- Wasn't nearly as influential as in the preliminary final. Missed a simple set shot in the fourth quarter that would have been scrutinised had the Lions not pulled one out of the fire.

7. Jarrod Berry, 6/10 -- Prolific and under pressure in the back half a lot in the first half. Was less involved as the game wore on but a contributor nonetheless with 17 disposals, six intercepts, and nine contested possessions.

8. Will Ashcroft, 8/10 -- Did what he always seems to do on Grand Final day. Finished with a game-high 31 disposals and nine clearances. Played his best footy in the final term (12 disposals) when the Lions needed him most.

9. Lachie Neale, 5.5/10 -- Enjoyed some clean moments at the contest but for the fourth straight final was well below his best. His third quarter easy set shot miss summed up his afternoon, really.

10. Levi Ashcroft, 6/10 -- Bounced back from an early shaky turnover to have a solid game. Booted a second quarter goal, took seven marks, and had 19 disposals at 90% disposal efficiency.

13. Logan Morris, 6.5/10 -- He was the hero with two goals at the death to snatch victory from the jaws of defeat. Kicked three and set up one of Lohmann's with a clever handball out of a contest.

15. Dayne Zorko, 7.5/10 -- Did a little bit of everything. Had a stack of footy early but struggled to use it efficiently. Finished with 28 disposals and nine marks, as well as seven tackles and seven intercepts.

16. Cam Rayner, 6.5/10 -- Had 18 disposals and more score involvements (8) than any of his Lions teammates and played his best footy late. Should have had a goal of his own in the first quarter but fluffed his lines.

22. Ty Gallop, 3.5/10 -- Looked shaky and totally out of his depth on Dockers spearhead Josh Treacy for much of the day. A pair of late intercepts saved him from a harsher rating.

23. Charlie Cameron, 8/10 -- Booted the first goal of the game (the first of three) and was electric throughout with his speed and cleanliness at ground level. He won countless one-on-ones and was just about as influential as anyone else on the ground.

26. Conor McKenna, 4.5/10 -- Kicked another miracle goal from a sharp angle and set up an important Lohmann goal but wasted a few other chances he'd nail on another day. Was the only Lion who failed to take a mark.

27. Darcy Gardiner, 3/10 -- Not sure he won a contest against Jye Amiss all day. Was beaten time after time and would be copping immense criticism if not for his team pulling off the most improbable late comeback.

30. Eric Hipwood, 3/10 -- Missed a couple of chances in the first half and was held to just one kick in the second. Finished up with a disposal efficiency of 33% from his six kicks.

31. Harris Andrews, 4.5/10 -- Didn't have a disposal in the first quarter, allowed Patrick Voss to kick three on him, and had the shocking turnover that led to the late Michael Fredrick goal. Having said that, he did have seven intercepts and 15 one percenters.

32. Darcy Fort, 4/10 -- Provided serviceable ruck relief to Draper. Didn't have many notable moments, good or bad.

33. Zac Bailey, 7/10 -- Was prolific and influential without being at his devastating best. Set up the important Charlie Cameron goal in the third quarter with a gut-busting run on the wing and snapped a brilliant goal of his own in the dying minutes.

35. Ryan Lester, 5/10 -- Was shaky and unsure early but his 2026 Grand Final will be remembered for that remarkable goal-saving tackle on Josh Treacy. A game-changing moment.

44. Darcy Wilmott, 6.5/10 -- Was a safe and reliable hand out of the back half all day. Used the ball by foot with elite efficiency and won five intercepts.

Fremantle
3. Caleb Serong, 8/10 -- Tireless all game and a beast around the contest. His 13 clearances and 17 contested possessions were both game-highs, as he consistently drove Fremantle forward.

5. Heath Chapman, 7.5/10 -- Calm and composed behind the footy, reading the play superbly and bravely leaving his man to impact contests. Five intercepts. Nearly flawless, aside from one holding-the-ball error.

6. Jordan Clark, 5.5/10 -- Kept quieter than usual but still found plenty of the footy in defence, finishing with 14 disposals and nine intercepts without having his usual influence. Seven turnovers, too.

8. Andrew Brayshaw, 6.5/10 -- Not flashy, but did plenty of the hard work that often goes unnoticed. His seven tackles and six clearances were more telling than his 16 disposals.

9. Luke Jackson, 7.5/10 -- Clearly won the ruck battle with 47 hitouts and 13 to advantage, driving Fremantle's dominance around the stoppages. Also won four clearances, and his two contested marks underlined his influence around the ground.

10. Shai Bolton, 8/10 -- A constant spark and Fremantle's biggest source of X-factor, finishing with a team-high 26 disposals and the Norm Smith Medal. His 58% disposal efficiency and scrappy forward 50 entries stopped this rating being higher.

13. Luke Ryan, 4/10 -- A shaky start featured uncharacteristic fumbles and some nervous moments in defence. Settled somewhat and had a few nice moments, but never had a major influence on the contest.

16. Murphy Reid, 6.5/10 -- A strong finals response given his previous performances, finishing with 21 disposals, six inside 50s, and a clever goal. He was crafty early but then faded as the game wore on. His ball use also let him down at times, with too many missed targets.

17. Judd McVee, 5.5/10 -- Started slowly and was beaten by Charlie Cameron early, but worked his way into the game. Six intercepts and six score involvements, plus a huge fourth-quarter smother on a Kai Lohmann set shot were his highlights.

18. Mason Cox, 4/10 -- Limited to 32% game time so was never able to get into it, with no marks and four hitouts. Wasn't beaten aerially when he was out there, and didn't have an impact outside of two effective disposals when given his chances.

20. Patrick Voss, 7.5/10 -- Played a crucial role on Harris Andrews, keeping the Brisbane star accountable and limiting his influence while making his own impact. Voss took important marks, laid strong tackles, and finished with three goals and eight score involvements from just nine disposals.

21. Oscar McDonald, 5.5/10 -- Another Freo defender who started shaky, but lifted when given more responsibility after captain Alex Pearce left the field injured. Finished with a game-high four intercept marks.

23. Karl Worner, 4.5/10 -- Some useful one-percenters and had 16 disposals with 529 metres gained, but he was outmuscled too often and had a few moments he'd rather forget.

24. Jye Amiss, 6/10 -- Amiss was good after not touching the footy in the first quarter. Finished with two goals from 10 disposals, but crucially won most one-on-ones when duelling with Darcy Gardiner. The Docker won that battle.

25. Alex Pearce, 3/10 -- A miserable afternoon for the skipper, who looked to be playing sore before leaving with an Achilles issue in the third term. Had little impact defensively and struggled to influence the game before that moment.

26. Hayden Young, 8.5/10 -- One of Fremantle's best all afternoon and a class above at times. Young combined his usual skill and power with a huge work rate, finishing with 22 disposals, nine tackles, and eight score involvements, while his two goals in the third term were both massive.

28. Neil Erasmus, 5.5/10 -- Had some clean and composed moments amid the chaos around him, using the ball neatly and generally doing his bit without having a consistent major influence.

32. Michael Frederick, 6/10 -- Worked tirelessly up and down the ground, constantly chasing and harassing his opponents. His four tackles showed the defensive effort, and he nailed a huge final-quarter goal.

34. Corey Wagner, 5/10 -- Played his usual half-back/wing role without doing anything particularly eye-catching.

35. Josh Treacy, 7/10 -- Treacy was excellent around the ground, taking three contested marks and regularly getting the better of Ty Gallop in the air. He finished with one goal but was a constant threat, though a costly brain-fade miss from directly in front in the final term will haunt him.

39. Sam Switkowski, 6/10 -- The retiring Switkowski stayed involved all game and played his usual hard-working defensive-forward role. Remained lively around the 50 applying pressure and creating opportunities while finishing with 16 disposals, six marks, and four tackles.

43. Isaiah Dudley, 6.5/10 -- A constant spark whenever he got near the ball, with 13 disposals and two stunning goals. Dudley took on opponents, dodged his way through traffic and made his moments count, although he had just one touch in the final term.

44. Matthew Johnson, 5/10 -- Had some good wins in and under but otherwise struggled to make his mark on the contest. A missed set shot in the final term was a chance to stamp himself on the game.

stories.headline: 2026 WNBA playoffs: Experts pick the first round, WNBA champion
stories.summary: We're picking every series in the WNBA playoffs' first round -- and our champions and Finals MVP. Who gets the edge?
stories.body:
The WNBA playoffs are here! With all four first-round series tipping off Sunday (first game starts at 2 p.m. ET), it's time to find out what the experts think about some of the best matchups of the 2026 postseason.

Will Napheesa Collier and Olivia Miles of the Minnesota Lynx take down the New York Liberty in a 2024 WNBA Finals rematch? Can Caitlin Clark's Indiana Fever slow down A'ja Wilson and the defending champion Las Vegas Aces? Will the upstart Golden State Valkyries win their first postseason game after being swept last year? Will the Atlanta Dream's Angel Reese impress against the Washington Mystics in her first postseason game?

There's plenty to watch, and we asked our WNBA analysts to break it all down.

Check out which teams our experts picked for every first-round series, as well as the Finals matchup, winner and MVP.

stories.headline: The performance bonuses for Van, Tsarukyan? Spots in P4P top 10
stories.summary: Former UFC champion puts elite status of women's flyweight division on display in ESPN's P4P top 10.
stories.body:
UFC 331 delivered some remarkable performances, a couple of which landed fighters in the ESPN pound-for-pound rankings.

One of them is not heavyweight Sean Sharaf, despite him pulling off the biggest upset in UFC history with his 12-second knockout of mega-prospect Gable Steveson. Women's flyweight Casey O'Neill produced a leading candidate for submission of the year, escaping a dangerous position to quickly armbar Eduarda Moura, but that didn't earn O'Neill a top-10 spot, either.

Both of those fighters were eye openers, but the rankings were reserved for the two winners of Saturday's headline fights.

In the main event, Joshua Van successfully defended his men's flyweight title against former champion Alexandre Pantoja, using crisp boxing and efficient grappling to secure a unanimous decision. Van moves into the men's rankings at No. 8, and Pantoja, who previously occupied that position, drops out.

Also earning a top-10 spot is co-main event winner Arman Tsarukyan, who knocked out flashy striker Mauricio Ruffy to all but secure a lightweight title shot. Tsarukyan moves in at No. 10, with former light heavyweight champion Alex Pereira falling from the rankings.

For the ESPN divisional MMA rankings, click here.

Note: Results are current; rankings are as of Sept. 23. To be eligible for the rankings, a fighter must have competed over the past 12 months or must have an upcoming fight booked. Fighters who have been dropped for inactivity can be reinstated only after they compete.

Men's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Islam Makhachev

UFC welterweight champion

Record: 29-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Ian Machado Garry, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Makhachev vacated the UFC lightweight championship to go for a second title at welterweight. By winning that belt last November with a thrashing of Jack Della Maddalena, Makhachev staked his place among MMA's greatest -- not just in today's sport but of all time. His win over Machado Garry at UFC 330 was his 17th straight, breaking the UFC record for consecutive wins. Makhachev is piling up unprecedented achievements.

2. Petr Yan

UFC bantamweight champion

Record: 20-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Merab Dvalishvili, Dec. 6, 2025

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Dvalishvili

What a return to the top it's been for Yan. He began his career with 15 consecutive wins before going on a 1-4 run from 2021 to 2023. That almost doesn't feel real now, after watching him reclaim his throne against Dvalishvili, who once handed him the worst loss of his career. Yan took a major detour, but this was the destination we felt he was capable of before the skid. He once again looks like one of the best fighters on the planet. He can prove it by beating Dvalishvili again.

3. Merab Dvalishvili

UFC bantamweight

Record: 21-5

Last: L (UD) vs. Petr Yan, Dec. 6, 2025

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Yan

Dvalishvili was on one of the most impressive runs through the UFC's bantamweight division ever. Not only did he defeat Sean O'Malley for the second time in nine months at UFC 316, but he showcased a new part of his game, finishing O'Malley with a guillotine. Starting in August 2022, Dvalishvili beat José Aldo, Yan, Henry Cejudo, O'Malley (twice), Umar Nurmagomedov and Cory Sandhagen. But at UFC 323, in an attempt to become the first champion in UFC history to successfully defend a title four times in a calendar year, Dvalishvili lost a rematch with Yan. They will fight for a third time at UFC 333.

T-4. Tom Aspinall

UFC heavyweight

Record: 15-3, 1 NC

Last: NC1 vs. Ciryl Gane, Oct. 25, 2025

Next: TBA

You can make a case that Aspinall is the most dynamic, skillful, talented heavyweight the sport has seen. He is dominating opponents in a way that is unmatched. No one can last a round with him. He had hoped to prove his supremacy against Jon Jones, but Jones opted to retire, elevating Aspinall from interim champion. His first defense of the undisputed belt ended anticlimactically, as an eye poke resulted in his UFC 321 fight with Gane being declared a no-contest. Still recovering from the eye injury, Aspinall vacated his title on Sept. 14.

T-4. Justin Gaethje

UFC lightweight champion

Previous ranking: 6

Record: 28-5

Last: W (TKO4) vs. Ilia Topuria, June 14

Next: TBA

Gaethje has spent his 15-year career thrilling MMA fans, but before the title bout on the White House lawn, all he had to show for it -- aside from 15 bonus checks in 15 UFC appearances -- were two missed opportunities to be an undisputed champion. His fourth-round TKO of Topuria got Gaethje over the hump. It was a resilient performance in a back-and-forth battle that is a prime candidate for fight of the year. More important for Gaethje: At age 37, he is finally sitting at the top of the mountain.

6. Ilia Topuria

UFC lightweight

Previous ranking: 5

Record: 17-1

Last: L (TKO4) vs. Justin Gaethje, June 14

Next: TBA

Topuria was an undefeated two-division champion when he ran into Gaethje at UFC Freedom 250 and was brutalized in a stoppage loss. How will that affect the immediate future of Topuria? His knockout wins over two of the greatest featherweights, Alexander Volkanovski and Max Holloway, gave him an intimidating aura. Can the former champion get that back?

7. Alexander Volkanovski

UFC featherweight champion

Record: 28-4

Last: W (UD) vs. Diego Lopes, Jan. 31

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Movsar Evloev

It felt as if the sport had started to write Volkanovski's eulogy following his knockout loss to Ilia Topuria in February 2024. Volkanovski noticed and made a point of proving to everyone he still has plenty left by recapturing the featherweight belt at UFC 314, the first of two consecutive wins over Lopes. His age (37) will likely continue to be a prefight topic, which is fine because Volkanovski enjoys proving people wrong. Can he hand Evloev his first loss at UFC 333?

8. Joshua Van

UFC flyweight champion

Previous ranking: Unranked

Record: 18-2

Last: W (UD) vs. Alexandre Pantoja, Sept. 19

Next: TBA

Van has been champion since December, but until UFC 331, there were doubters. Van had been handed the belt by default, when his challenge for the title was waved off after 26 seconds because Pantoja dislocated his left elbow. Van went on to defend the title against Tatsuro Taira in May, then faced Pantoja in a rematch this past weekend. Van produced a clear victory -- his eighth win in a row -- to leave no doubt who rules at 125 pounds.

9. Ciryl Gane

UFC heavyweight champion

Record: 14-2, 1 NC

Last: W (TKO2) vs. Alex Pereira, June 14

Next: Nov. 14 vs. Josh Hokit

Gane is unique in that he is the first -- and could very well go down as the only -- heavyweight to face the division's four biggest names in Francis Ngannou, Jon Jones, Tom Aspinall and Pereira. None of those four have fought each other, yet all four have have fought the Frenchman. Gane was 0-2 with a no-contest against that group before he knocked out Pereira in the second round of their interim title fight. Gane was elevated to undisputed champ after Aspinall, still injured, vacated his title, and the new champ will defend against Hokit at UFC 334.

10. Arman Tsarukyan

UFC lightweight

Previous ranking: Unranked

Record: 24-3

Last: W (KO1) vs. Mauricio Ruffy, Sept. 19

Next: TBA

Tsarukyan is right back in the place he was in January 2025 -- on the cusp of a title fight. He withdrew from that challenge of Islam Makhachev one day before UFC 311 because of a back injury, and later in the year he was passed over twice when the UFC was booking lightweight title bouts. But by knocking out Mauricio Ruffy with an elbow in the first round at UFC 331, Tsarukyan put himself back at the front of the line.

Other fighter receiving votes: Alex Pereira.

How our panel voted
Brett Okamoto: 1. Islam Makhachev; 2. Petr Yan; 3. Merab Dvalishvili; 4. Ilia Topuria; 5. Alexander Volkanovski; 6. Joshua Van; 7. Arman Tsarukyan; 8. Ciryl Gane; 9. Alex Pereira; 10. Justin Gaethje.

Carlos Contreras Legaspi: 1. Makhachev; 2. Volkanovski; 3. Gaethje; 4. Topuria; 5. Pereira; 6. Dvalishvili; 7. Van; 8. Gane; 9. Yan; 10. Tsarukyan.

Andrew Davis: 1. Makhachev; 2. Tom Aspinall; 3. Yan; 4. Dvalishvili; 5. Gaethje; 6. Topuria; 7. Volkanovski; 8. Van; 9. Gane; 10. Tsarukyan.

Dre Waters: 1. Makhachev; 2. Aspinall; 3. Yan; 4. Dvalishvili; 5. Gaethje; 6. Volkanovski; 7. Topuria; 8. Van; 9. Gane; 10. Pereira.

Jeff Wagenheim: 1. Makhachev; 2. Aspinall; 3. Yan; 4. Van; 5. Gaethje; 6. Dvalishvili; 7. Tsarukyan; 8. Topuria; 9. Gane; 10. Volkanovski.

Women's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Valentina Shevchenko

UFC flyweight

Record: 26-4-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Zhang Weili, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

Shevchenko's dominance came under question in 2022 and 2023, when she went 1-1-1 in a trilogy with Alexa Grasso. Boy, does that feel like a long time ago now. Shevchenko more than reasserted herself as the best flyweight in the world, and then she established herself as the No. 1 woman in the world, period. It wasn't surprising that she beat Zhang, but it was surprising how easy she made it look. Shevchenko is out injured, however, so she has vacated her UFC title, which will be up for grabs when Natalia Silva meets Wang Cong on Oct. 3.

2. Zhang Weili

UFC flyweight / strawweight

Record: 26-4

Last: L (UD) vs. Valentina Shevchenko, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

It's hard to move up in weight, especially at the highest level. That sounds like it should be obvious, but Zhang had been dominant at 115 pounds for so long, some of us might have taken for granted how big of a challenge moving to 125 would be. UFC 322 was a bad night for Zhang, but she doesn't have many. And if she decides to stay at flyweight, it certainly seems reasonable to believe she'll fare better in the future.

3. Cris Cyborg

PFL featherweight champion

Record: 30-2, 1 NC

Last: W (UD) vs. Ketlen Vieira, Aug. 22

Next: TBA

It had been a while since Cyborg had fought an elite opponent in MMA until she met Larissa Pacheco in 2024. That was a legitimate matchup -- and many within the industry were predicting Cyborg's downfall. Instead, she took out the PFL's two-weight champion, upending all of Pacheco's momentum. One of the original pioneers of women's MMA is once again a champion after getting her second career submission at PFL Lyon in December. The PFL promoted her fight with Vieira as a retirement bout, but after her win Cyborg did not sound like someone who is done fighting.

4. Mackenzie Dern

UFC strawweight champion

Record: 17-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Gillian Robertson, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Dern's rise to the 115-pound throne was truly a changing of the guard. She is the division's first first-time champion since 2019, because the previous three champs -- Zhang Weili, Carla Esparza and Rose Namajunas -- all were in their second reigns. Dern, nearly a decade into her MMA career after multiple jiu-jitsu world championships, has won four fights in a row, including a dominant performance against a fellow grappling-heavy fighter, Robertson, in her first title defense.

5. Natalia Silva

UFC flyweight

Record: 20-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Rose Namajunas, Jan. 24

Next: Oct. 3 vs. Wang Cong

Silva is looking every bit the part of a future UFC champion following a dominant display against Alexa Grasso at UFC 315 and a victory over Namajunas at UFC 324. Silva's stick-and-move style has frustrated even the highest level of opponent, and she's got youth on her side as she won't turn 30 until 2027. With an injured Valentina Shevchenko having vacated the title, Silva will fight Wang for the belt at UFC 332.

6. Alexa Grasso

UFC flyweight

Previous ranking: 10

Record: 18-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Manon Fiorot, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Grasso went nearly three years without winning a fight, but her 2023 win right before the skid was a huge one, a submission of Valentina Shevchenko for the UFC title. What followed were two more fights with Shevchenko -- a draw, then a loss -- and then a loss to Natalia Silva. But she reasserted herself with a finish of Maycee Barber in March, then got the best of Fiorot, a fellow title contender, at Noche UFC to put herself in position for another title shot.

7. Dakota Ditcheva

PFL flyweight

Record: 16-0

Last: W (UD) vs. Denise Kielholtz, July 31

Next: TBA

Not only did Ditcheva win the PFL's flyweight season in 2024, but she did so in spectacular fashion -- a TKO finish over Taila Santos, who once challenged for a UFC title. Ditcheva fought only once in 2025, dominating Sumiko Inaba in the co-main event of the first PFL Champions Series card in Cape Town, South Africa. She then spent over a year on the sideline, healing injuries to both hands, before returning at PFL New York with a dominant win over Kielholtz.

8. Manon Fiorot

UFC flyweight

Previous ranking: 6

Record: 13-3

Last: L (UD) vs. Alexa Grasso, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Fiorot had handled everyone the UFC put in front of her -- except the champion, Valentina Shevchenko, who defeated the Frenchwoman at UFC 315 in May 2025. But then, with another title shot within her grasp, Fiorot ran into Grasso, a former champion, at Noche UFC and lost a competitive fight.

9. Erin Blanchfield

UFC flyweight

Previous ranking: 8

Record: 14-2

Last: W (Sub2) vs. Tracy Cortez, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: Oct. 17 vs. Jasmine Jasudavicius

Her rise toward the top of the division was derailed by a March 2024 loss to Manon Fiorot, but Blanchfield bounced back with two straight wins, including one over two-time former strawweight champion Rose Namajunas in November 2024. If she wins her October bout with Jasudavicius, a fellow top-10 flyweight contender, Blanchfield would inch ever closer to a title shot.

10. Tatiana Suarez

UFC strawweight

Previous ranking: 9

Record: 12-1

Last: W (Sub2) vs. Loopy Godínez, April 11

Next: TBA

If Suarez is still feeling the effects of last year's humbling defeat to Zhang Weili in a title challenge, she certainly didn't show it at UFC 327, overcoming early adversity to thrash Godinez, a fellow top-10 strawweight. Suarez is going to be a tough out for anyone at 115 pounds.

How our panel voted
Brett Okamoto: 1. Valentina Shevchenko; 2. Zhang Weili; 3. Mackenzie Dern; 4. Cris Cyborg; 5. Alexa Grasso; 6. Manon Fiorot; 7. Dakota Ditcheva; 8. Natalia Silva; 9. Erin Blanchfield; 10. Tatiana Suarez.

Carlos Contreras Legaspi: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Cyborg; 3. Zhang; 4. Dern; 5. Silva; 6. Grasso; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Suarez; 9. Fiorot; 10. Blanchfield.

Andrew Davis: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Zhang; 3. Cyborg; 4. Dern; 5. Silva; 6. Grasso; 7. Blanchfield; 8. Ditcheva; 9. Suarez; 10. Fiorot.

Dre Waters: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Zhang; 3. Cyborg; 4. Silva; 5. Dern; 6. Grasso; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Blanchfield; 9. Fiorot; 10. Suarez.

Jeff Wagenheim: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Zhang; 3. Cyborg; 4. Silva; 5. Grasso; 6. Dern; 7. Fiorot; 8. Blanchfield; 9. Suarez; 10. Ditcheva.

stories.headline: Victor Radley cleared, Roosters sweating on Connor Watson
stories.summary: Victor Radley has learnt his grand final fate after a hip-drop tackle, while Connor Watson is hoping to be cleared to play for the Sydney Roosters.
stories.body:
Connor Watson could still feature in the NRL grand final for the Sydney Roosters, with the Tri-colours set to kick off the process of clearing concussion protocols for the decider.

The Roosters were breathing a sigh of relief on Saturday morning, with Victor Radley avoiding a suspension for his hip-drop tackle on Herbie Farnworth in the 36-20 preliminary-final win over the Dolphins.

Radley can enter an early guilty plea and pay a $2000 fine, which would clear him to play in next Sunday's decider against Penrith or Newcastle.

But the bigger headache for the Roosters may be Watson.

The super sub had been on the field for just 60 seconds when his head collided with Dolphins forward Kulikefu Finefeuiaki's hip in the 31st minute at Suncorp Stadium on Friday.

The knock was originally ruled as a category two by the Roosters, before that was overruled by the independent doctor, who deemed it a category one.

That ruled Watson out of the game and triggered an 11-day stand-down that would keep him out of next Sunday's decider in Sydney.

But Trent Robinson said post-game Watson was undergoing more tests, with the coach refusing to rule out seeking an exemption for the NSW Origin utility.

"That was a hard one; he came out as a category two, they changed it to a one after a couple of minutes," Robinson said.

"That's still 'watch this space' on Connor. It depends on how his tests go (if the Roosters appeal), so we'll see how that goes."

Watson is the first player at risk of missing an NRL grand final under the 11-day stand-down run, which was introduced in 2023.

Penrith had faced the potential of a similar situation last year, when Scott Sorensen suffered a head knock in their preliminary final loss to Brisbane.

Sorensen was also deemed to be a category two by club medical staff, before the NRL's independent doctor classed it as a category one.

Had Penrith won the match, it is understood they would have appealed to have Sorensen play in the grand final.

There have been multiple instances this year of players challenging category one concussions and being able to play the next week.

However Watson would still need to prove he was wrongly classified and be asymptomatic from Saturday morning, among several other requirements.

In more positive news for the Roosters, Sam Walker emerged unscathed after a record-equalling 27-day comeback from a syndesmosis injury.

The halfback left the field early with the match decided, but not before delivering a masterclass in orchestrating his backline.

The Roosters have not lost a grand final under Robinson, who will now be angling for his fourth premiership as a coach in the club's first decider since 2019.

"It's mostly internal, you want to get the most out of it," he said of the pressure to return to the big stage.

"I know what my role is ... it's not about getting into a grand final, it's about winning it.

"That's pretty simple and that's what I'm here to do."

stories.headline: 2026 NBA buzz: Latest free agency and trade updates
stories.summary: We're tracking deals, trades and buzz across the NBA, including Steph Curry's new extension with the Warriors.
stories.body:
NBA free agency has almost reached the end, with several players landing in new homes this offseason.

LeBron James decided to continue his historic career with the Philadelphia 76ers after months of deliberation. The Sixers also traded for Jaylen Brown this summer, turning the franchise into a true contender with two huge moves.

Meanwhile, Giannis Antetokounmpo is headed to South Beach to team up with Bam Adebayo and the Miami Heat, and the Los Angeles Lakers have been sold for the second time in 10 months.

What will happen next during this turbulent offseason?

Check back here for all the latest buzz, news and reactions from our ESPN NBA insiders, with the latest info at the top:

Quick links:

Free agency grades | Trade grades

Trade tracker | Transactions

Depth charts | Trade machine | More

Sept. 25

What's next for Curry and the Warriors?

Stephen Curry's two-year, $116 million extension made him the first player in NBA history to amass $600 million in career on-court earnings.

The deal has also put the Golden State Warriors in a position to have extra spending power next summer.

By Curry taking $10 million less than the maximum allowed, the Warriors project to have nearly $38 million in cap space in 2027. Golden State could increase its projection to $55 million if center Kristaps Porzingis is waived in the offseason. Porzingis' $20 million salary for next season is guaranteed for $3 million.

For Golden State to have ample room, forwards Draymond Green and Jimmy Butler III would need to sign elsewhere or at a significantly lesser salary. Both players are free agents next summer.

Both salary projections include the $17 million free agent hold of guard Brandin Podziemski. The former first-round pick is eligible until Oct. 19 to extend his contract. -- Bobby Marks

Grading the Curry deal: Why Warriors don't get an A

Grizzlies waive D'Angelo Russell

The Memphis Grizzlies have waived D'Angelo Russell, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Russell has made one All-Star team during his career and was selected No. 2 in the 2015 NBA draft.

Sept. 23

Sources: Status of Mavs big man Lively up in air
Dallas Mavericks center Dereck Lively II has not been cleared for training camp and his status for the start of the regular season has yet to be determined as he continues to recover from right foot surgery, sources told ESPN's Tim MacMahon.

After playing a key role as a rookie in the Mavericks' run to the 2024 NBA Finals, Lively's promising career has been derailed by recurring problems with his right foot, which has been surgically repaired twice in the last 14 months.

Lively is ramping up toward being cleared for basketball activity, sources said, emphasizing that the team is not discouraged by his progress. Dallas begins training camp on Saturday.

Extension unlikely as Knicks, Towns talks stall
Talks have stagnated between the New York Knicks and Karl-Anthony Towns on a contract extension, and an agreement is considered unlikely as the team begins training camp next week, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania and Vincent Goodwill on Wednesday.

The sides have spent extensive time discussing a potential extension during the offseason, but there has been no movement lately in negotiations, sources said, as the Knicks stand to go for a repeat following their first NBA title in 53 years.

Sept. 22

Charania: Hield, Nembhard to Charlotte for Finney-Smith
The Atlanta Hawks are trading Dorian Finney-Smith to the Charlotte Hornets for Buddy Hield, Ryan Nembhard and cash, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.

Leonard, Raptors agree to two-year extension
The Toronto Raptors and Kawhi Leonard have agreed to a two-year, $115 million extension, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Leonard now has a total of three years and $165 million left on his deal.

The 2026-27 season will be Leonard's first back in Toronto since the 2018-19 campaign, a season in which he helped lead the Raptors to their only title in franchise history.

Sept. 21

Charania: Pistons, Duren at an "impasse"
Free agent center Jalen Duren and the Detroit Pistons are at an impasse this season and the franchise is uncertain if he will show up to next Monday's Media Day, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.

"When you talk to people close to [Duren], he feels a certain way toward the Pistons' respect level for him," Charania said on NBA Today. "For him it's been all about respect, for the team it has just been about business. ... Over the course of this offseason, his offer has been been around the $180 to $190 million over five years range. And that has also included incentives like weight clauses to my understanding. And that has all played a part in this as well.

"Over the last several weeks it's kind of quiet on this front. The sides have picked up communication. And I am told right now the Pistons offer to Jalen Duren is $200 million over five years."

Duren has until Oct. 1 to sign a qualifying offer.

Hawks' Henri Veesaar out with torn ACL

The Atlanta Hawks announced that center Henri Veesaar tore his ACL during a Sept. 15 workout. He will undergo surgery in October and is expected to miss the entire 2026-27 season.

Sept. 18

Pistons, Thompson reach five-year, $155 million extension
Detroit Pistons All-Defensive forward Ausar Thompson has agreed to a five-year, $155 million rookie-scale contract extension with the franchise, sources told ESPN.

Thompson lands the fully guaranteed extension after making first-team All-Defense and finishing third in Defensive Player of the Year voting last season. The 23-year-old averaged 9.9 points, 5.7 rebounds, 3.1 assists and 0.9 blocks in 2025-26 while leading the NBA in steals per game (2.0).

Heat, Larsson agree to four-year, $60 million extension
Miami Heat guard Pelle Larsson has agreed to a new four-year, $60 million contract extension, with a mutual option for the 2030-31 season, Austin Brown and Steven Heumann of CAA Sports told ESPN on Friday.

A second-round find in the 2024 draft, the 6-foot-5 guard avoids restricted free agency next summer and locks in a new deal with a mutual option that fully guarantees $60 million while allowing either side to opt in on 2030.

Jazz, George agree on a five-year, rookie-scale extension
Utah Jazz guard Keyonte George have agreed on a five-year, $157.5 million rookie-scale contract extension with the franchise, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania and Tim MacMahon. George was the No. 16 pick in the 2023 draft and has averaged 17.2 points and 5.3 assists per game in his three seasons with the Jazz.

Sept. 17

Bey, Pelicans agree to three-year extension
New Orleans Pelicans' Saddiq Bey agreed to a three-year, $55.5 million contract extension with the franchise, plus a trade kicker, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Bey averaged a career-high 17.7 points per game last season after missing all of the 2024-25 season with a torn ACL.

Sept. 16

Kings remain interested in Duren
The Sacramento Kings continue to loom in the background of Jalen Duren's restricted free agency with the incumbent Detroit Pistons.

Kings general manager Scott Perry met with Duren for dinner in Miami in early July and has maintained a level of steady interest in the ultimate outcome of Duren's free agency, though a path to acquire Duren this summer remains blocked.

The Pistons declined any legitimate conversation about a Duren sign-and-trade to the Kings for starting center Domantas Sabonis and have maintained a strong stance about their intention to keep Duren.

Warriors keeping roster spot open for LeBron
The Golden State Warriors enter the second week of July yet to sign an outside free agent.

They were among the group of teams registering a level of interest in veteran wing Rui Hachimura and scoring guard Anfernee Simons, league sources said, but didn't meet the ultimate price point for a contract on either.

Simons went off the board to the Philadelphia 76ers for two years and $12.3 million -- nearly the same contract the Warriors gave to De'Anthony Melton.

They opted to retain Melton instead of putting more behind a pursuit of Simons, team sources said, because of a belief that Melton better fits the backcourt needs of the healthiest version of their current roster. He's not as explosive a scorer but is a more versatile and effective perimeter defender and pairs well with Stephen Curry.

Hachimura's contract terms (two years, $28 million to the LA Clippers) also came in higher than the Warriors proved willing to stretch. They have limited financial flexibility after bringing back Al Horford and Kristaps Porzingis, keeping space for Draymond Green to ultimately return and continuing their slow pursuit of LeBron James.

On the James front, Warriors sources continue to express a low level of optimism that James will ultimately pick them as his next team, but they intend to keep roster space open for James until he ultimately declares his choice. -- Anthony Slater

Expect Monday to be the busiest day on the NBA calendar
Starting at 12:01 p.m. ET, the moratorium will be lifted, meaning the trades that are sending Giannis Antetokounmpo to Miami, Jaylen Brown to Philadelphia, Kawhi Leonard to Toronto and LaMelo Ball to Minnesota can be finalized.

The timeline of trade calls is comparable to waiting on the runway for takeoff. Each trade has a designated time slot for its call, starting early in the afternoon and lasting into the evening. Keep in mind however that players involved in trades must report and pass a physical for a trade to become official.

Trades are not the only transaction that can become official. All player contracts negotiated and agreed upon can be finalized. For example, the Hornets can officially ink Coby White to the three-year, $74 million contract that had been reported.

Teams are also allowed to begin signing players that are extension-eligible. The list of notable players eligible on Monday include Nikola Jokic, Karl-Anthony Towns, Victor Wembanyama, Amen and Ausar Thompson and Cason Wallace. Donovan Mitchell is eligible starting Tuesday.

One more item to watch is restricted free agents, notably Peyton Watson and Jalen Duren.

If either player signs an offer sheet prior to noon ET, his prior team will have until 11:59 p.m. ET on July 7 to match. If the offer sheet comes in after noon ET, his prior team has until 1:59 p.m. ET on July 8 to match. -- Bobby Marks

Who could the Kings draft at seventh overall?
The Sacramento Kings' long-standing interest in Arkansas guard Darius Acuff Jr. is an open secret in the NBA. If Acuff is there at No. 7, it's widely expected that general manager Scott Perry will select him.

There's mutual interest. Acuff came to Sacramento for an in-person meeting with the organization's coaching staff and decision-makers earlier this month and would be delivered an immediate high-usage role. He would eventually get the keys to the offense for a young rebuilding team in transition.

But there's no guarantee he'll make it to the Kings. Acuff met with the LA Clippers, selecting No. 5, and there's at least some level of interest, though he isn't considered the favorite to land in a backcourt that already includes Darius Garland.

The Brooklyn Nets, at No. 6, are a wild card. The latest buzz has them more often tied to Louisville guard Mikel Brown Jr. and Tennessee wing Nate Ament, but everything with Brooklyn (including the possibility of a trade) is unpredictable, and it's possible Acuff could be off the board in the sixth slot.

Team sources maintain that the Kings are comfortable with the patient approach, waiting for Acuff to fall to No. 7 but also lining up alternative plans. They attempted to get Brown and Illinois guard Keaton Wagler into town for a visit. Both prospects canceled those plans.

Why Dolan is so worried about the second apron
The New York Knicks' championship parade has not even started, but there are already questions over whether finances will break up the roster.

"If we could bring back the whole team, exactly as is, why wouldn't you?" Knicks owner James Dolan said Wednesday on WFAN's "Carton Show." "I don't know if we'll be able to.

"We're willing to stretch, but there's certain things in the NBA that you'd have to be suicidal to do. One of them is the second apron. Cannot go into the second apron."

Including the 24th pick in next week's draft (June 23 and 24, 8 p.m. ET on ABC/ESPN), New York is $13 million below the second apron and has decisions with free agents Landry Shamet, Mitchell Robinson and possibly Jose Alvarado. (Alvarado has until Monday to decide on his $4.5 million option.) The entire starting five, meanwhile, is under contract through at least 2026-27. Karl-Anthony Towns is extension-eligible this summer and can become a free agent in the 2027 offseason if an agreement is not reached.

The second apron is a punitive luxury tax threshold restricting how teams add to their rosters in free agency, trades and the draft. In the case of the Knicks, the team would not be allowed to send cash in a trade, use the $6.1 million tax midlevel exception, aggregate salaries in a trade or use more than 100% of the traded player exception.

A team cannot trade its first-round pick seven years out if it finishes over the second apron in consecutive seasons, which no team has ever done. That same pick could be moved back to the end of the first round if a team finishes over the second apron in three out of four seasons. Luckily for Dolan and the Knicks, there are no rules that prohibit a team from retaining its own players.

New York can exceed the threshold to sign Robinson, Shamet and Alvarado. If the Knicks let the three players sign elsewhere, they would have their first-round pick (New York also has the 31st and 55th picks in the second round), the $6.1 million tax midlevel exception and $2.5 million veteran minimum exceptions available as replacements.

Since the apron rules were implemented before the 2024-25 season, Cleveland, Phoenix, Minnesota and Boston have finished the regular season over the second apron. The Knicks finished the past two seasons $53,000 and $370,000 below. Next offseason, New York is projected to be $31 million below the second apron with seven players under contract. -- Bobby Marks

Edwards out weeks as injuries mount for Wolves

The Minnesota Timberwolves won the battle on Saturday night, with a stirring Game 4 victory over Denver that brought the team within a win of the second round.

But they might have lost the war.

On Saturday night, ESPN's Shams Charania reported that Donte DiVincenzo had torn his right Achilles and would miss the rest of the postseason. And on Sunday morning, he reported that four-time All-Star Anthony Edwards would miss multiple weeks after hyperextending his left knee.

Losing a starting backcourt in one fell swoop would hurt any team in the playoffs, but it should be especially tough on Minnesota. The Timberwolves rely on a strong core, with little depth behind it; entering Saturday's games, only seven Wolves had averaged more than 10 minutes per game in the playoffs. By comparison, 10 members for both the Oklahoma City Thunder and San Antonio Spurs played more than that, and even the injury-riddled Lakers had eight.

With Edwards and DiVincenzo out, Minnesota's entire rotation and offensive gameplan will shift. Ayo Dosunmu -- fresh off a 43-point outburst -- and Bones Hyland are the likely replacement starters, with some combination of Mike Conley, Terrence Shannon Jr. (who received his first playoff minutes in Game 4) and Kyle Anderson receiving more minutes off the bench.

That might not be a tenable arrangement on offense, unless Dosunmu can continue posting career highs in points going forward. There's very little shooting and playmaking talent left in Minnesota's lineup, and Julius Randle -- who has been only OK against Denver, averaging 17.5 points and 3.5 assists per game on subpar efficiency -- will need to step up in Edwards' stead.

But all isn't lost for the Timberwolves, at least against the Nuggets. Surprisingly, lineups without DiVincenzo and Edwards held their own in the regular season, with a plus-3.0 net rating, per Cleaning the Glass (which removes garbage time). Those groups excelled on defense. And as long as Rudy Gobert and Jaden McDaniels remain on the floor, Minnesota will retain its top two options to guard Nikola Jokic and Jamal Murray, respectively.

Minnesota is already winning because of its defense. The Timberwolves have a 112.3 offensive rating in the playoffs, which is worse than their regular-season mark (115.6). But they've held the Nuggets, who led the league with a 121.1 offensive rating in the regular season, to just 105.2 points per 100 possessions in the playoffs.

It might not be the most probable outcome, but they have a real chance to keep Denver's offense sufficiently in check to sneak out one more win in three tries.

Beyond that, Minnesota is likely in trouble. Without Edwards for multiple weeks, the Timberwolves might need to hope that the Portland Trail Blazers upset San Antonio to have a chance to reach the conference finals for the third consecutive season. -- Zach Kram

Minnesota Timberwolves guard Donte DiVincenzo will miss the rest of this postseason and at least a large chunk of next season after tearing his right Achilles just over a minute into Game 4 against the Denver Nuggets. The injury was first reported by ESPN's Shams Charania.

It's difficult to say whether that injury is a bigger blow to the Timberwolves or to DiVincenzo's own career path.

He was one of just four players in the NBA to start all 82 games, and he offered a skill set otherwise missing from the players who surround Anthony Edwards in Minnesota's starting lineup. DiVincenzo shot 38% on 3-pointers this season and made 3.0 per game, which is more than Julius Randle, Jaden McDaniels and Rudy Gobert combined.

The Timberwolves had a plus-6.0 net rating with DiVincenzo on the court in the regular season, versus a minus-2.0 mark without him. That was the largest differential on the team. And in a very small sample of three playoff games, that gap widened: Minnesota was plus-20.7 with DiVincenzo and minus-26.3 without him.

Ayo Dosunmu fit in well in Minnesota after arriving via midseason trade, and he will presumably replace DiVincenzo in the starting lineup for the remainder of Minnesota's playoff run. Dosunmu is an accurate shooter (44% on 3s this season) but on much lower volume, and defenses are less likely to worry about him on the perimeter. According to the new "average gravity" statistic at NBA.com, DiVincenzo ranked in the 77th percentile among qualified players this season, while Dosunmu was in the 56th percentile.

And although the Timberwolves' starting unit might not be compromised too severely with Dosunmu in DiVincenzo's place -- if Edwards, who also left Saturday's Game 4 early, is also out for an extended period, then the Timberwolves will be severely compromised regardless -- the ripple effects could be catastrophic for Minnesota's bench. In the first three games against the Nuggets, only seven Timberwolves averaged more than 10 minutes per game: the five starters, Dosunmu and former Sixth Man award winner Naz Reid.

Why LaMelo's flagrant 2 falls into a gray area
The NBA retroactively assessed Charlotte Hornets guard LaMelo Ball with a flagrant foul 2 for tripping Miami Heat center Bam Adebayo in Tuesday's Eastern Conference play-in game, which Charlotte won in overtime thanks to Ball's last-second layup.

But for the Heat and their fans, it doesn't erase Adebayo's injury, it doesn't remove Ball from Friday's 8-9 game against the Orlando Magic and it all but certainly won't impact the Hornets should they reach the first round.

That's because one quirk of the tournament's addition is that, not unlike the NBA Cup title game, the play-in tournament lives as its own statistical entity. They are neither playoff nor regular-season games, with no bearing on postseason and regular-season stats or awards.

That's also the case with flagrant foul points, which can have a massive impact when they start to add up. In 2016, Draymond Green was suspended for Game 5 of the NBA Finals for accumulating four flagrant points over the course of the postseason, something that helped Cleveland pull off its stunning 3-1 comeback.

While the Hornets' playoff stay isn't likely to last as long -- Charlotte needs to win Friday just to set up a first-round meeting with the top-seeded Detroit Pistons -- Ball entering the playoffs with two flagrant points would have at least given heft to the belated punishment.

Instead, the decision felt fairly hollow. And in asking sources around the league Wednesday ahead of the NBA's announcement that Ball wouldn't be suspended, opinions were mixed. Some argued that a hefty fine would suffice, because you shouldn't retroactively remove him from the next game because of Adebayo's unfortunate injury. Others argued the opposite, saying he should have to sit out Friday's win-and-in showdown.

None of it, however, will reverse the agonizing end to Miami's season.

"I'm not really thinking about that anymore," Heat coach Erik Spoelstra told reporters Thursday during the team's exit interviews. "I don't think [Ball] is a dirty player. It should have been caught in the moment, and it wasn't. And you move on." -- Tim Bontemps

The NBA's take on tanking

ESPN's Anthony Slater talked to players, coaches and executives about how they feel about tanking in the NBA and the future it has in the league.

In ESPN's conversations with dozens of players, coaches and front office executives, a consistent theme emerged: Nobody likes it -- "I hate it," Golden State Warriors coach Steve Kerr said -- but not many deny it is often the most prudent team-building path when stuck near the bottom. Different seasons and different drafts will generate different forms, but everyone agrees it'll continue until the NBA figures out either the proper rules or punishments to curb it.

"These teams are doing the whole gamut: sitting guys in the fourth, playing analytically bad lineups, drawing up plays for bad shots," one Western Conference general manager said. "The creativity is impressive and I don't blame them. It's the best strategy to get better. Look at all the most promising teams in the league: Thunder, Spurs, Pistons, Rockets, Hornets. Years of being bad and building up on high picks. It's painful but worthwhile."

The strategies are growing in audaciousness and frequency of use. The orders from management are coming in earlier in the season, creating months of competitively compromised and often unwatchable basketball. The average margin of victory in NBA games this season is 13.1 points, the largest spread in history, and a record 89 games have been decided by 30 or more points.

What NBA players, coaches and execs are saying about tanking

Hoop Collective: Bulls changes and playoff seeding battles

April 7

Bulls hiring search firm for front office replacements
The Chicago Bulls are expected to engage a search firm in order to find a replacement for vice president Arturas Karnisovas and general manager Marc Eversley, whom the team fired after six seasons running the basketball operations department, sources told ESPN.

It's a different approach from the process Chicago used when it hired Karnisovas in 2020. Team president and CEO Michael Resindorf said then that he targeted the top "No. 2" in basketball and went after general managers such as Karnisovas, who was then with the Denver Nuggets, and Bobby Webster, who was then general manager of the Toronto Raptors, but has since been promoted to their head of basketball operations.

This is only the second time since 2003 that the Bulls have hired a new head of basketball operations. Before Karnisovas got the job in 2020, John Paxson assumed the role for 17 years from 2003 to '20. Karnisovas and Eversley went 224-254 across six seasons leading the organization to one winning season and one playoff appearance.

Even though Chicago sits 29-49 and in 12th place in the Eastern Conference, the opening is expected to be an attractive one around the league. The Bulls have flexibility on how they can build their roster with their own lottery pick, approximately $60 million in cap space and young players on the roster without long-term salary commitments.

Chicago is still expected to try to retain coach Billy Donovan in some capacity after the season. -- Jamal Collier

Bulls fire Karnisovas, Eversley

The fractured relationship between Giannis and the Milwaukee Bucks
ESPN's Shams Charania went inside the drama between two-time MVP Giannis Antetokounmpo and the Milwaukee Bucks, as a crucial summer window approaches. The story details what has led to the falling out in Milwaukee and what it means for the future of both Antetokounmpo and the Bucks.

This season, the Bucks have gone 17-19 with Antetokounmpo in the lineup and 14-28 without him, and they rank 25th in offensive rating and 26th in defensive rating overall. They are one of six NBA teams to rank in the bottom five in both categories.
All the while, the uncertainty of Antetokounmpo's future in Milwaukee lingered. The Bucks engaged in trade talks ahead of the Feb. 5 trade deadline but chose to hold on to him, even as it became increasingly clear that they didn't have much hope of even elevating into the play-in race. Milwaukee is now headed to the draft lottery for the first time since 2016, snapping a streak of nine consecutive years in the playoffs. The Bucks haven't won a postseason series since 2022. Antetokounmpo, who is under contract for one more season, has played in a career-low 36 games and privately feuded with the organization for several months, culminating in rebuking the team's requests to shut down in the final month of the season and setting up another contentious summer.

"When your best player is one foot in, one foot out," said one team source, "you're not going to win."

The Bucks have officially been eliminated from the playoffs.

Inside the Bucks' lost season

Bulls part ways with front office leaders, Karnisovas and Eversley
The Chicago Bulls have dismissed the executive vice president of basketball operations Arturas Karnisovas and general manager Marc Eversley after six seasons, per ESPN's Shams Charania.

The 29-49 Bulls sit in 12th in the East and are bound for the lottery.

The North Carolina Tar Heels are expected to hire former Denver Nuggets coach Michael Malone for the same position with the school, per ESPN Pete Thamel.

Malone won the 2022-23 NBA championship with the Nuggets.

How the Tar Heels got here, what he'll need to do to succeed

Brian is joined by ESPN's Tim Bontemps and Tim MacMahon to discuss Cooper Flagg's big weekend and where the Rookie of the Year award race currently stands. Williamson unlocks more money in 61st game
New Orleans Pelicans forward Zion Williamson has reached another financial benchmark for games played.

The salary protection for his $42.2 million salary in 2026-27 was nonguaranteed headed into the season. But now that he has played in 61 games, 80% ($33.7 million) of his $42.2 million salary for next season is protected.

The remaining $8.4 million will become guaranteed if Williamson's combined body weight and body fat percentage is less than 295. There were seven times he was required to weigh in this season. It's unclear what he weighed during those check-ins.

Williamson has one of the league's most unusual contracts. His salary next season and in 2027-28 originally became nonguaranteed when he missed more than 22 games in the 2022-23 season. His $44.9 million salary in 2027-28 remains nonguaranteed.

The 61 games played this season is tied for the third most in his career. He's averaging 21.1 points and 5.7 rebounds per game. The Pelicans, who have been eliminated from playoff contention, have four games left on their schedule. -- Bobby Marks

One big question facing every lottery team's offseason

April 3

Doncic out for the rest of the regular season
Los Angeles Lakers star Luka Doncic is out indefinitely with a Grade 2 right hamstring injury, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania and Dave McMenamin. Doncic will miss the rest of the regular season, and his availability for the playoffs is uncertain.

In the 20 minutes after the news broke, the Lakers' title chances dropped from 30-1 to 100-1, per DraftKings Sportsbook.

Doncic, who has played in 64 games and ranked fourth in ESPN's latest MVP straw poll, will apply for what's called an "extraordinary circumstances challenge" to the 65-game rule for award consideration, per his agent, Bill Duffy.

Per ESPN's Bobby Marks, Doncic can apply the exception for the two games he missed in December for the birth of his daughter. The application must be made no earlier than 12 p.m. ET on the last day of the regular season and no later than 11:59 p.m. on the day after the last day of the regular season.

Doncic signed a three-year extension last August and has been named All-NBA in five of the six previous seasons.

There will be no financial implications in his next contract if the application is denied.

Though the Lakers haven't provided a timeline for his return, Grade 2 hamstring injuries typically require a monthlong recovery. Doncic has averaged a league-high 33.5 points this season, along with 7.7 rebounds and 8.3 assists.

The Lakers, who have gone 8-2 in their past 10 games, are third in the Western Conference, one game ahead of the No. 4-seeded Denver Nuggets, 2.5 games ahead of the No. 5-seeded Houston Rockets and 3.5 ahead of the No. 6-seeded Minnesota Timberwolves.

In the scenario Maxey is named All-NBA this season, he would become eligible to sign a four-year, $300 million supermax extension in the 2027 offseason if he is also named All-NBA next season. The first year of the extension would begin in 2029-30.

A player with seven or eight years of NBA service is supermax eligible if they are named All-NBA in the immediately preceding season or in two of the immediately preceding three seasons. Maxey ranks fourth in the league in points per game (28.8) and third in total clutch points. -- Bobby Marks

stories.headline: Lando Norris: Drivers should have 'one-race ban' after collision with Franco Colapinto at Azerbaijan GP
stories.summary: Lando Norris has said there are "drivers that shouldn't be in Formula 1" and that Franco Colapinto should be banned for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix pile-up which ended his race.
stories.body:
Lando Norris has said Franco Colapinto should be banned for the pile-up which ended his Azerbaijan Grand Prix, adding "[there's] some drivers that shouldn't be in Formula 1."

Colapinto wiped out Norris and his own Alpine teammate Pierre Gasly from the race at a Safety Car restart on lap 36, locking up and going down the inside of Turn 1.

Norris had dropped down the order with a lock-up of his own earlier in the race, leaving him battling in the midfield at the restart.

The reigning world champion pointed the finger of blame at Colapinto, hinting that the Argentine driver does not deserve his spot on the grid.

"I was just slow," Norris told Sky Sports after the Baku race. "Struggled a lot in this race. You saw how quickly everyone came past me.

"Otherwise, I still made the mistake. But at the end of the day, I just got taken out. Just some drivers that shouldn't be in Formula 1 to, be honest."

Colaptino was handed a 10-second time penalty for the incident, and was later given a five-place grid penalty for the next race in Malaysia, as he did not make it to the end of the race.

He and teammate Gasly had been running strongly -- after the incident, Gasly was broadcast saying: "Oh my god. Oh my god. I cannot believe it. So many [censored] points gone!"

Speaking to the written press, Norris doubled down, suggesting Colapinto should be banned for the next race.

As quoted by PA, Norris said: "If you cause a crash on a restart like this, you should have at least a one-race ban.

"I just got taken out. And the FIA should be stricter by starting to hand out bans for this kind of stuff.

- Azerbaijan Grand Prix: George Russell fights off Max Verstappen to take dominant win

- Max Verstappen says he prefers F1 not to race in Middle East due to ongoing conflict

- Azerbaijan Grand Prix results: George Russell takes commanding victory in Baku - as it happened

"It is just careless. It costs a lot of money, all my parts are in the bin now. It is not driving that deserves to be in Formula 1.

"In Formula 1 you would expect that drivers can anticipate that the grip will be low and tyre temperatures are low.

"You want to be against the best drivers and when stuff like this happens it is because, yeah, they shouldn't be there."

Colapinto, who was recently given an Alpine contract extension for 2027, accepted responsibility, apologising to his team and teammate, as well as Norris.

"Just sorry to all the team, not only to Pierre, it was a big mistake," Colapinto said. "Big sorry to Pierre, he has been working really hard in the factory. We lost a lot of positions and we were with both cars in the points.

"Very sad and disappointed. Big, big sorry, it's a big mistake. Cold brakes, cold tyres, I was completely out of control. Unfortunately, I also took Pierre out. And Lando of course. Big sorry to both of them."

The incident might raise fears of what the social media backlash will be.

Ahead of the weekend, Gasly revealed the threats he, his girlfriend and family members had received after he held up Colapinto in the closing stages of the Madrid Grand Prix.

Colapinto has built a big fanbase back home in Argentina since his debut in 2024.

Asked about the partnership with Gasly, Colapinto said: "We are good. We've always been quite good together. Since we worked together for the first time, we got on very well. So we need to move on."

Gasly appeared unmoved when told about Colapinto's apology, reflecting on the big points loss in the championship.

"I can't find my words," Gasly said. "It's not easy. We did a very good weekend and the car was one of the best race cars we've had this season. And the pace was great. Keeping up with Lewis [Hamilton] and Lando for most of the race. And we had a 14 or 15 second gap to the midfield."

When asked if the partnership was still in a good place, Gasly said: "Respect. It's all about respect. As long as there is respect, everything is possible."

Speaking in the top-three news conference about Norris' comments, race winner George Russell disagreed with the fellow Brit.

Russell said: "Yeah, I think that's too harsh, personally. I think Safety Car restarts, cold tyres, a very small mistake can have big consequences. And from what I saw today, that's what it looked like. It was a small error that had a big consequence. I think, personally, race bans should come from drivers intentionally doing something very dangerous and very reckless. So I think it was unfortunate."

Four-time world champion Max Verstappen agreed with Russell and added: "Yeah, I think as long [as], of course, the driver that caused it is aware of what he did, right, and apologised. And, I mean, yeah, that happens.

"I mean, like, a small mistake or misjudgement, you lock up, it's on the inside, low grip, and, of course, then I guess a bit unfortunate that it involves so many cars. But, yeah, unfortunate, happens, and it's not nice, I think. Not nice for anyone involved, right? But like George said, I think, yeah, a race ban probably is a bit much."

stories.headline: Embolo out of Switzerland squad over fake COVID-19 documents
stories.summary: World Cup quarterfinalist Switzerland has lost a second player from its Nations League squad because of years-old cases of fake COVID-19 documents.
stories.body:
BERN, Switzerland -- World Cup quarterfinalist Switzerland has lost a second player from its Nations League squad because of years-old cases of fake COVID-19 documents.

Breel Embolo will not join the squad in Scotland as planned, the Swiss soccer federation said Friday, due to fresh reporting in national media about his past case of obtaining forged test certificates in 2021.

- Embolo: People in Europe 'shocked' at MLS move

- Embolo debut goal gives Atlanta draw at Miami

"This decision aims to allow the team to remain fully focused on the next matches," the federation said about the Atlanta United forward.

Switzerland captain Granit Xhaka agreed with team officials last weekend to withdraw from the squad because he is implicated in an investigation of a doctor issuing fake vaccination certificates during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Xhaka, the Swiss record holder with 152 caps, admitted getting the forged document in 2022 and accepted he made mistakes.

Switzerland starts its Nations League second-tier group Saturday at North Macedonia, plays at Scotland on Tuesday, then has home games in Lucerne against Slovenia and North Macedonia.

Embolo already was suspended for the game Saturday because of his controversial red card against Argentina in the World Cup quarterfinals.

Soccer's Zurich-based rules panel, known as IFAB, later acknowledged Embolo was mistakenly sent off in a breach of video review protocol.

On Friday, the Switzerland Today outlet reported details of Embolo's financial sanction imposed last year for the previously known false test result documents.

At the World Cup, the 29-year-old Embolo scored in Switzerland's opening game -- a 1-1 draw with Qatar -- despite arriving at the tournament days later than teammates because of a visa issue with United States authorities. He also scored in a round of 32 win over Algeria.
